question: What cancer type and cancer stage are most ideal for using image-guided surgery as a treatment option?

ingredients.name: answer_critical_0
ingredients.criterion: The answer defines IGS (also fluorescence-guided surgery) as a surgical intervention using fluorescence/NIR imaging for real-time intraoperative identification of tumor margins, distinguishing malignant from healthy tissue.
examples: IGS uses fluorescence imaging to identify tumor margins in real time during surgery
Fluorescence-guided surgery relies on NIR imaging agents to visualize malignant vs. healthy tissue intraoperatively

ingredients.name: answer_critical_1
ingredients.criterion: The answer identifies breast cancer as the most ideal cancer type for IGS, specifically in the context of breast-conserving surgery (BCS/lumpectomy) at initial surgery.
examples: IGS was developed to meet an unmet need in the management of breast cancer at initial BCS

ingredients.name: answer_critical_2
ingredients.criterion: The answer states that early-stage disease is the most ideal stage, with justification: early-stage breast cancer treated by BCS/lumpectomy, sentinel lymph node mapping in early-stage cervical/endometrial cancer, or early-stage solid tumors to reduce recurrence and metastasis risk.
examples: Early stage, since early-stage breast cancer is treated with BCS/lumpectomy
Early-stage cervical and endometrial cancer for sentinel lymph node mapping
Early-stage solid tumors, to reduce the chance of recurrence and metastasis

ingredients.name: answer_critical_3
ingredients.criterion: The answer explains the rationale: IGS addresses positive margins and the ~20% re-excision rate in BCS, with ~85% of re-excisions due to initial positive margins; surgeons relying on visual and tactile cues risk residual lesions.
examples: Re-excision rate is ~20%, with ~85% due to positive initial margins
Surgeons relying on visual and tactile cues may leave residual lesions, motivating intraoperative imaging

ingredients.name: answer_critical_4
ingredients.criterion: The answer cites at least two additional cancer applications of IGS/fluorescence from the passages: advanced epithelial ovarian cancer, neuro-oncology, prostate, head and neck, liver, or rectal cancer.
examples: Advanced epithelial ovarian cancer for detecting microscopic peritoneal metastases
Neuro-oncology resection to the functional limit with greater extent of resection
Head and neck cancer to better define resection borders

ingredients.name: valuable_0
ingredients.criterion: The answer states that IGS improves the chance of complete resection with negative margins, citing the rectal cancer navigation study (R0 rates 93% vs 84% in LARC; 79% vs 49% in LRRC) and its demonstrated cost-effectiveness.
examples: Navigated surgery achieved 79% R0 resections in LRRC vs 49% with standard surgery
Navigation in rectal cancer was shown to be early cost-effective

ingredients.name: valuable_1
ingredients.criterion: The answer contrasts IGS with current practice, which relies on visual/tactile cues and preoperative imaging (MRI, mammography, ultrasound, CT) that cannot guide intraoperative decisions, leaving an unmet intraoperative need.
examples: Surgeons rely primarily on visual and tactile cues, risking residual lesions
Traditional imaging modalities are used preoperatively but not intraoperatively

ingredients.name: valuable_2
ingredients.criterion: The answer notes that outcomes depend on the specificity and half-life of the imaging agent, and/or that FDA-approved NIR devices and dyes exist (e.g., ICG, firefly camera in the da Vinci platform), reflecting the field's technical maturity.
examples: Surgical outcome depends on the specificity and half-life of the imaging agent
ICG is an FDA-approved NIR dye commonly used
FDA-approved devices exist for NIR fluorescence navigation in laparoscopic and robotic surgery
